title: Novel association of ocular myasthenia gravis with Brown syndrome in an adult
case_prompt:
A 45-year-old woman presented with an 8-day history of binocular vertical diplopia and a subjective restriction in elevation. Her medical history was notable for hypothyroidism and polycystic ovarian syndrome; she had no prior ocular surgery or trauma. On examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 6/4.5 bilaterally, intraocular pressures were normal, and pupils were equal and reactive. Extraocular motility testing showed mild (–1) limitation of elevation in adduction of the left eye with pain on right gaze, and cover testing revealed a left hypotropia of 4 prism diopters. Anterior and posterior segment exams were unremarkable.

A contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain and orbits demonstrated normal superior oblique muscles and trochlear tendon complexes. Given suspicion for acquired Brown syndrome of inflammatory origin, she was started on ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily. Five days later, she returned with increased trochlear-region pain and worsening diplopia. Examination revealed moderate (–2) limitation of elevation in adduction of the left eye; other findings were stable. Oral prednisolone 25 mg daily was initiated, with subjective pain relief but persistent motility deficit.

One month after presentation, her motility deficit progressed to bilateral moderate (–2) elevation limitation in adduction. A repeat orbit MRI again showed no superior oblique hypertrophy, tendon inflammation, or trochlear attachment abnormalities. Rheumatology evaluation and serologic testing for mixed connective tissue disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and rheumatoid arthritis were negative. She remained symptomatic over the next 11 months while receiving up to 50 mg daily of oral prednisolone, which was tapered and replaced with methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Congenital Brown syndrome — “Congenital Brown syndrome is secondary to anomalies at birth to the trochlear apparatus, superior oblique (SO) muscle or SO tendon” (adult onset without congenital anomalies).  
2. Autoimmune connective-tissue–associated Brown syndrome — “acquired forms of Brown syndrome can result from autoimmune disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), scleroderma, or rheumatoid arthritis” (serologic tests were negative).  
3. Scarring or trauma-induced Brown syndrome — “Scarring from previous surgical procedures or trauma to the SO tendon as well as inflammatory processes are also potential causes of Brown’s syndrome” (no history of surgery or trauma).  
4. Idiopathic Brown syndrome — “Bilateral idiopathic Brown syndrome typically presents in children aged between 2 and 8 years as opposed to adults” (atypical demographic and sequential bilateral onset).  
5. Inflammatory tenosynovitis — “Generally, MR imaging of patients with acquired Brown’s demonstrates abnormal thickening of the SO tendon” (MRI remained normal on two occasions).  
6. Mixed connective tissue disease, SLE, or rheumatoid arthritis — “serology for mixed connective tissue disease, SLE, and rheumatoid arthritis was negative.”  
7. Ocular myasthenia gravis — “Ocular myasthenia gravis should be a differential in any patient presenting with vertical strabismus presenting as Brown syndrome” (revealed by later ptosis, limb weakness, positive acetylcholine receptor antibodies, and response to pyridostigmine).
